source_text: Ἐπεὶ τοίνυν φασί τινες εἰκόνας μὲν εἶναι ταύτας, θεοὺς δὲ ἐφ᾿ οἷς αἱ εἰκόνες, καὶ τὰς προσόδους ἃς ταύταις προσίασι καὶ τὰς θυσίας ἐπ᾿ ἐκείνους ἀναφέρεσθαι καὶ εἰς ἐκείνους γίνεσθαι, μὴ εἶναί τε ἕτερον τρόπον τοῖς θεοῖς ἢ τοῦτον προσελθεῖν (χαλεποὶ δὲ θεοὶ φαίνεσθαι ἐναργεῖς), καὶ τοῦ ταῦθ᾿ οὕτως ἔχειν τεκμήρια παρέχουσι τὰς ἐνίων εἰδώλων ἐνεργείας, φέρε ἐξετάσωμεν τὴν ἐπὶ τοῖς ὀνόμασι δύναμιν αὐτῶν. Δεήσομαι δὲ ὑμῶν, μέγιστοι αὐτοκρατόρων, πρὸ τοῦ λόγου ἀληθεῖς παρεχομένῳ τοὺς λογισμοὺς συγγνῶναι· οὐ γὰρ προκείμενόν μοι ἐλέγχειν τὰ εἴδωλα, ἀλλὰ ἀπολυόμενος τὰς διαβολὰς λογισμὸν τῆς προαιρέσεως ἡμῶν παρέχω. Ἔχοιτε ἀφ᾿ ἑαυτῶν καὶ τὴν ἐπουράνιον βασιλείαν ἐξετάζειν· ὡς γὰρ ὑμῖν πατρὶ καὶ υἱῷ πάντα κεχείρωται, ἄνωθεν τὴν βασιλείαν εἰληφόσι (βασιλέως γὰρ ψυχὴ ἐν χειρὶ θεοῦ, φησὶ τὸ προφητικὸν πνεῦμα), οὕτως ἑνὶ τῷ θεῷ καὶ τῷ παρ᾿ αὐτοῦ λόγῳ υἱῷ νοουμένῳ ἀμερίστῳ πάντα ὑποτέτακται. Ἐκεῖνο τοίνυν σκέψασθέ μοι πρὸ τῶν ἄλλων.Οὐκ ἐξ ἀρχῆς, ὥς φασιν, ἦσαν οἱ θεοί, ἀλλ᾿ οὕτως γέγονεν αὐτῶν ἕκαστος ὡς γινόμεθα ἡμεῖς. Καὶ τοῦτο πᾶσιν αὐτοῖς ξυμφωνεῖ· Ὁμήρου μὲν γὰρ λέγοντος· Ὠκεανόν τε, θεῶν γένεσιν, καὶ μητέρα Τηθύν, Ὀρφέως δὲ (ὃς καὶ τὰ ὀνόματα αὐτῶν πρῶτος ἐξεῦρε καὶ τὰς γενέσεις διεξῆλθε καὶ ὅσα ἑκάστοις πέπρακται εἶπε καὶ πεπίστευται παρ᾿ αὐτοῖς ἀληθέστερον θεολογεῖν, ᾧ καὶ Ὅμηρος τὰ πολλὰ καὶ περὶ θεῶν μάλιστα ἕπεται) καὶ αὐτοῦ τὴν πρώτην γένεσιν αὐτῶν ἐξ ὕδατος συνιστάντος· Ὠκεανός, ὅσπερ γένεσις πάντεσσι τέτυκται. Ἦν γὰρ ὕδωρ ἀρχὴ κατ᾿ αὐτὸν τοῖς ὅλοις, ἀπὸ δὲ τοῦ ὕδατος ἰλὺς κατέστη, ἐκ δὲ ἑκατέρων ἐγεννήθη ζῶον δράκων προσπεφυκυῖαν ἔχων κεφαλὴν λέοντος, διὰ μέσου δὲ αὐτῶν θεοῦ πρόσωπον, ὄνομα Ἡρακλῆς καὶ Χρόνος. Οὗτος ὁ Ἡρακλῆς ἐγέννησεν ὑπερμέγεθες ὠόν, ὃ συμπληρούμενον ὑπὸ βίας τοῦ γεγεννηκότος ἐκ παρατριβῆς εἰς δύο ἐῤῥάγη· τὸ μὲν οὖν κατὰ κορυφὴν αὐτοῦ οὐρανὸς εἶναι ἐτελέσθη, τὸ δὲ κατενεχθὲν γῆ. Προῆλθε δὲ καὶ θεὸς Γῆ διὰ σώματος· Οὐρανὸς δὲ Γῇ μιχθεὶς γεννᾷ θηλείας μὲν Κλωθώ, Λάχεσιν, Ἄτροπον, ἄνδρας δὲ ἑκατόγχειρας Κόττυν, Γύγην, Βριάρεων, καὶ Κύκλωπας Βρόντην καὶ Στερόπην καὶ Ἄργον· οὓς καὶ δήσας κατεταρτάρωσεν, ἐκπεσεῖσθαι αὐτὸν ὑπὸ τῶν παίδων τῆς ἀρχῆς μαθών. Διὸ καὶ ὀργισθεῖσα ἡ Γῆ τοὺς Τιτᾶνας ἐγέννησε. Κούρους δ᾿ οὐρανίωνας ἐγείνατο πότνια Γαῖα, Οὓς δὴ καὶ Τιτῆνας ἐπίκλησιν καλέουσιν, Οὕνεκα τισάσθην μέγαν Οὐρανὸν ἀστερόεντα.
thought_title: The Gods Themselves Have Been Created
pass_a_gloss: For certain people say that these are images, and that the gods are those upon whom the images are, and that the approaches which they make to these and the sacrifices are offered to those and are made to them, and that there is no other way for the gods to be approached, for the gods are seen to be harsh and evident. And they provide proofs of this, that the idols of some have energies. Come, let us examine the power that is in their names. I will ask you, greatest emperors, to forgive my thoughts before I speak the truth; for it is not my intention to accuse the idols, but having been freed from the slanders, I provide the reasoning of our choice. You have from yourselves also the heavenly kingdom to examine; for just as all things have been entrusted to you, father and son, having received the kingdom from above, as the prophetic spirit says, 'the soul of a king is in the hand of God', so all things have been subjected to the one God and the Word, His Son, unbroken. Consider this for me before the other things. The gods were not from the beginning, as they say, but each of them has come to be just as we are born. And this is in agreement with all of them; for Homer says: 'Ocean, the genesis of the gods, and their mother Tethys', and Orpheus, who first discovered their names and told their genesis and all that has been done to each of them, and is considered to theologize more truthfully among them, and whom Homer also follows in many things, especially about the gods, and he establishes their first genesis from water: 'Ocean, who has been generated as the genesis of all things'. For water was the beginning, according to him, of all things, and from the water, mud was established, and from both, a living dragon was born, having a lion's head, and in the middle of them, a god's face, named Hercules and Chronos. This Hercules generated a huge egg, which, being filled by the power of the one who generated it, was broken into two from friction; the upper part of it was made to be the heaven, and the lower part, the earth. And the goddess Earth came forth through the body; and Heaven, having mingled with Earth, generated females, Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos, and males, the hundred-handed, Cottys, Gyges, and Briareus, and the Cyclopes, Brontes, Steropes, and Argos; whom, having bound, he threw down, having learned that he would be overthrown by his children from power. And so, the Earth, being angry, generated the Titans. And the mistress Earth generated the heavenly youths, whom they call Titans, because they avenged the great Heaven, the starry one.

pass_b_english: Some people claim that these statues are mere images, that the gods are the beings they represent, and that the honors and sacrifices offered to the images are actually transferred to those gods; they insist there is no other way to approach the gods, who appear harsh and unapproachable, and they point to the supposed miraculous powers of certain idols as proof. Let us examine, then, the power inherent in their names. Greatest Emperors, I ask you to pardon my frankness before I speak the truth; my purpose is not to accuse the idols, but, having been freed from slander, to present the reasoning behind our choice. You yourselves possess the heavenly kingdom to scrutinize; for just as all things have been entrusted to you, father and son, who received the kingdom from above — as the prophetic Spirit says, "The soul of a king is in the hand of God" — so all things have been subjected to the one God and His Word, the Son, understood as an unbroken unity. Consider this first, before all else. The gods did not exist from the beginning, as is claimed; rather, each came into being just as we are born. All their traditions agree on this. Homer says, "Ocean, the genesis of the gods, and their mother Tethys." Orpheus, who first invented their names, detailed their origins and deeds, and is regarded among them as the more truthful theologian — Homer himself follows Orpheus in most matters, especially concerning the gods — and Orpheus establishes their first origin from water: "Ocean, who has been generated as the genesis of all things." According to him, water was the beginning of all things; from water came mud, and from both was born a living dragon with a lion's head and, in the middle, a god's face, named Hercules and Chronos. This Hercules generated an enormous egg, which, filled by the force of its begetter, burst in two from friction; the upper half became heaven, the lower half earth. Then the goddess Earth emerged through a body; Heaven mingled with Earth and begot females — Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos — and males — the hundred-handed Cottys, Gyges, and Briareus, and the Cyclopes Brontes, Steropes, and Argos. He bound them and cast them into Tartarus, having learned he would be overthrown by his own children. Consequently, Earth in anger begot the Titans. The noble Earth brought forth the heavenly youths, whom they call Titans, because they avenged great starry Heaven.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex mythological genealogy and the theological argument regarding the nature of the gods. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Greek. Scripture citation (Proverbs 21:1, though not explicitly named in the Greek, is correctly identified by the translator as 'the prophetic spirit says' in both versions) is handled according to the rules. The translation of 'ἐναργεῖς' as 'evident' (Pass A) and 'unapproachable' (Pass B) are stylistic variations that do not violate the sense of the Greek. The translation of 'κατεταρτάρωσεν' as 'threw down' (Pass A) and 'cast them into Tartarus' (Pass B) is acceptable as the latter provides the etymological context of the verb.

The Greek text is accurately translated, with no omissions, additions, or distortions. All key terms and concepts are preserved, and the scriptural and doctrinal content is faithfully rendered. The translation maintains the original's argumentation and theological distinctions.
